spots.name: Ellis Park Stadium
spots.label: Ellis Park Stadium

text.geographic_location: Ellis Park Stadium is in Doornfontein, an inner-city district in the south-east of Johannesburg. It is the centrepiece of a sports area that includes Johannesburg Stadium, Standard Bank Arena and the Ellis Park Tennis Stadium.
text.access_note: Photos from the stands need a match ticket or a stadium tour, so check the official site before you go for access and any photography rules.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so plan to arrive from Doornfontein or central Johannesburg by car or ride-hail. Ask to be dropped at the stadium entrance for your event or tour. Check current local security advice before you go, and avoid walking to the stadium on match days. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
Ellis Park Stadium is Johannesburg's great rugby and football ground, and the phone icon on the map puts you inside it, looking over the pitch from the stands. It is best known as the venue of the 1995 Rugby World Cup final, won by the Springboks. The ground was rebuilt in the early 1980s and holds almost 60,000 people. Its story goes back further: it was built in eight months on a former quarry and rubbish-dump site in Doornfontein, and the first test there was played in June 1928. It is named after J. D. Ellis, who helped make the land available.

From the seats, the stadium photographs well because of its scale. You can fit the pitch, the curve of the stands and the crowd into one frame, and on a match day the colour and noise of the supporters make the picture. Open-air concerts are also held here, which gives other chances for atmosphere shots.

The stands are not open to casual visitors. You need a match ticket or a stadium tour, and the rugby museum that comes with the tour is open on days without a match. If you only have access outside, the main stand facade framed by the surrounding Doornfontein streets is a worthwhile alternative. Rules on flash or larger equipment can apply during events, so check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The best views come from the seats inside the bowl, which need a match ticket or a stadium tour. From the seats the photo shows the pitch, the full stands and the crowd. If you cannot get inside, the exterior view of the main stand facade, with the Doornfontein streets around it, is the second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A match day gives the most atmosphere inside the stands. On a non-match day, the tour and museum give calmer conditions for photographing the empty seats and pitch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pitch to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or floodlights are washing out. Try a Live Photo on a match day to catch the crowd moving. Panorama can work for the whole bowl if you move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the pitch and the full sweep of the stands. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the crowd, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the players, banners or the far stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the pitch markings up with them, so the horizon of the stands stays level. Keep some of the crowd in the foreground to show the scale. If you shoot the outside instead, step back far enough to fit the whole facade in and include a little of the street for context.

spots.name: FNB Stadium
spots.label: FNB Stadium

text.geographic_location: FNB Stadium is in Nasrec, bordering the Soweto area of Johannesburg. It stands next to SAFA House, the South African Football Association headquarters.
text.access_note: The area around the stadium may be open to walk around, but access may change on event days, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Nasrec, on the border of Soweto, and then for the stadium. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m north-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description: FNB Stadium, also called Soccer City or the Calabash, is the big football and rugby stadium on the edge of Soweto, in the Nasrec area of Johannesburg. It was rebuilt for the 2010 FIFA World Cup, and the shape is meant to echo an African pot, which is where the nickname comes from. That is why it photographs so well. The outside is a mosaic of fire and earthen colours, with a ring of lights around the base that suggests a fire under the pot. Ten dark vertical lines also break up the stands. With a capacity of 94,736 it is the largest stadium in Africa, and it hosted the 2010 World Cup Final between the Netherlands and Spain. It also has a place in South Africa's political history. Nelson Mandela made his first Johannesburg speech here after his release in 1990, and a memorial service for him was held here on 10 December 2013. The stadium is so large that the main challenge is fitting it in. Stand back far enough to show the curve of the walls and the colours of the cladding, and keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines. Then move closer and fill the frame with the mosaic pattern for a second, more abstract shot. People walking past in the foreground help show how big the building is.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The building is huge, so frame what is visible from there, moving only where access allows.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the cladding. Around dusk, the ring of lights around the base is easier to capture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the cladding to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. If the lights around the base are on at dusk, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of the curved walls. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the mosaic cladding and the vertical lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone level with the gridlines switched on so the walls do not lean. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full bowl and keep the lower edge of the frame just below the ring of lights. For a detail shot, zoom in on the mosaic colours and the dark vertical lines.

spots.name: Carlton Centre
spots.label: Carlton Centre

text.geographic_location: The Carlton Centre is in the central business district of Johannesburg, on Commissioner Street. It is a large superblock of offices and shops that includes the tower.
text.access_note: The tower can be photographed from the surrounding public streets, but access to the building and any viewing areas may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Johannesburg, the central business district, and head for Commissioner Street, where the tower stands. Once you are on the street, the tower is easy to spot above the surrounding buildings. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description: The Carlton Centre is a 50-storey tower in the middle of central Johannesburg, and it is one of the easiest landmarks in the city to recognise. It stands 223 metres tall, and when it was finished in 1973 it was the tallest building in Africa. It held that title for 46 years. Today it is the fifth tallest on the continent, and The Leonardo, also in Johannesburg, now ranks above it. The tower is built of concrete with a grey granite finish, so it looks plain, solid and strongly vertical. That makes it a good subject for a phone, because the shape reads clearly even in a small picture. The complex also reaches a long way underground, with a shopping level below street level, so most of what you see from the pavement is the tower itself rising out of a city block. The tower is very tall, so the main challenge is fitting it in. Stand back as far as you comfortably can, switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and keep the phone as upright as possible. Switch on the gridlines and keep the tower's edges parallel to the vertical lines so it does not lean in the frame. Any people or vehicles at street level give a sense of scale. Keep your phone in a safe grip, as is sensible in any city centre.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, step back along the pavement as far as is comfortable, and use the ultra-wide lens until the full height of the building fits in your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the whole tower is lit evenly. A clear morning or afternoon gives you a plain blue sky behind the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky does not wash out and the concrete keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the tower in from close range. Use the default lens (1x) from further back for less stretching at the edges. Telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the top floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn gridlines on and line up the tower's edges with the vertical lines. Hold the phone as upright as you can, because tilting it back makes the tower lean inwards. Include any people or vehicles at street level for scale. A 2x-5x shot of the top floors makes a good second picture.
